title: Lecture #3: Java Variables & Data Types Explained
topics: Number systems (binary, octal, hex) in literals

questions.question: In the statement `int firstNum = 10;`, which description of each part matches the lecture's terminology?
options: `int` is the identifier, `firstNum` is the literal, and `10` is the data type
`int` is the data type, `firstNum` is the identifier (name of the container), and `10` is the literal stored in it
`int` is a literal, `firstNum` is a keyword, and `10` is the identifier
`firstNum` is the data type, `int` is the identifier, and `10` is the literal
questions.explanation: The notes describe a variable as a named container in memory: the name (`firstNum`) is the identifier, the value placed in the container (`10`) is a literal, and `int` is the data type that decides what the container can hold. `int` is a reserved keyword naming a type, so it can never be an identifier.

questions.question: Why is Java's `char` 16 bits wide instead of the 7/8 bits that ASCII needs?
options: Because a char also stores the string length alongside the character
Because Java stores every character twice for error checking
Because Java chars use Unicode, which covers characters beyond English (such as Hindi letters), not just ASCII's 0-127
Because 16 bits makes char arithmetic faster than int arithmetic
questions.explanation: The notes contrast ASCII (0 to 127: a-z, A-Z, 0-9, punctuation) with Unicode, which Java uses so a char can hold characters from many languages, e.g. Hindi letters; hence char = 16 bits. Nothing about length or duplication is stored in a char; it simply holds one UTF-16 code unit.

questions.question: You need a variable to hold the current world population (about 8,100,000,000). Which integer type from the lecture's table is the smallest one that can hold it?
options: byte
short
int
long
questions.explanation: int is 32 bits with a maximum of 2,147,483,647 (about 2.1 billion), so 8.1 billion does not fit; long (64 bits, up to about 9.2 x 10^18) does. int is the tempting answer because it is the default integer type, but its range is far too small here.

questions.question: This snippet is adapted from the lecture's Demo.java. What does it print?
options: Compile error: consecutive underscores are not allowed in a literal
questions.explanation: Underscores between digits are only for readability; the compiler ignores them, and any number of consecutive underscores is legal as long as they sit between digits. A double this large is printed in scientific notation (6.022E23), not as a long string of zeros.

questions.question: With 8 bits you can write 2^8 = 256 patterns, so the largest unsigned value is 2^8 - 1 = 255. Why, then, is the range of a Java `byte` -128 to +127?
options: Because one bit of every byte is reserved by the JVM for garbage collection
Because every integer type in Java is signed, so the 256 patterns are split between negative and non-negative values
Because Java bytes are actually 7 bits wide
Because the value 128 is reserved to mark the end of a byte array
questions.explanation: The notes stress that every number is signed in Java: the 256 patterns cover -128..-1 and 0..127, i.e. -2^7 to 2^7 - 1. A byte really is 8 bits wide (see the width table), so the reduced positive maximum comes from signedness, not from fewer bits.

questions.question: Inside `main`, a teammate writes `int x;` and on the next line `System.out.println(x);`. What happens?
options: Compile error: variable x might not have been initialized, because it was only declared, never given a value
It prints 0, because int variables always start at 0
It prints a random leftover value from memory, like in C
It throws a NullPointerException at runtime
questions.explanation: `int x;` is only a declaration (a 32-bit container is reserved); a definition such as `x = 4;` puts a value in it. Java refuses to compile a read of a local variable that has no value yet, so it neither prints 0 (that default applies to fields, not locals) nor exposes garbage memory like C.

questions.question: A teammate writes `float price = 5.23;` and gets a compile error. What is the cause and a correct fix?
options: float cannot hold decimals; use int price = 5.23 instead
The value is too large for 32 bits; use long price = 5.23L
A semicolon is not allowed after a decimal literal; remove it
A decimal literal like 5.23 is a double by default; write 5.23f (single precision) or declare price as double
questions.explanation: Real-number literals default to double (64-bit, double precision), and putting a double into a 32-bit float could lose precision, so Java demands the f suffix, exactly as the lecture's code does with 10.5_4f. 5.23 is tiny compared with float's range, so size is not the problem.

questions.question: Exactly one of these declarations fails to compile. Which one?
questions.codeSnippet:
int a = 1___000;            // Line 1
byte b = 0b0111_1111;       // Line 2
double d = 6.02_2e23;       // Line 3
long l = 3412_56_789_L;     // Line 4
options: Line 1
Line 2
Line 3
Line 4
questions.explanation: An underscore must sit between two digits, so placing one right before the L suffix (789_L) is illegal. Line 1 is fine (several underscores in a row are allowed), and Line 2 is binary 0111 1111 = 127, which fits in a byte's -128..127 range.

questions.question: Keywords are words reserved by Java. Which of these declarations compiles?
options: `int goto = 5;`
`int const = 5;`
`int Class = 5;`
`int void = 5;`
questions.explanation: Java is case-sensitive, so `Class` is just an ordinary identifier, while `void` is a keyword. `goto` and `const` are the trap: the notes point out they are reserved keywords even though Java never uses them, so they still cannot be variable names.
